material_systems.name: Clear Wood Sealer / Water Repellent

sealer.type: Penetrating clear water repellent — no UV pigment
products: Thompson's WaterSeal Advanced Clear Wood Protector
sealer.notes: Minimal UV protection — wood grain fully visible, natural appearance. Water repellent only. Best for new cedar/redwood where natural grain is desired. Shortest maintenance cycle (12-18 months, annual recoat). Single application — re-apply at 12-18 month intervals. No primer required — sealer penetrates directly into wood fibers.

material_systems.notes: Economy/minimal protection tier. No color matching required. Fastest to apply. Lowest material cost per gallon but shortest cycle drives higher lifetime cost. Coverage varies significantly by wood porosity: new smooth PT pine ~250 SF/gal, weathered porous cedar ~150 SF/gal.

material_systems.name: Semi-Transparent Penetrating Stain

stain.type: Penetrating semi-transparent stain with iron oxide UV pigments
stain.notes: PROFESSIONAL STANDARD for residential decks (~60% of professional deck staining work). Iron oxide pigments provide UV protection while allowing wood grain visibility. Penetrating chemistry soaks into wood fibers — erodes gradually rather than peeling. 2-3 year maintenance cycle. Easy maintenance recoat (clean and recoat, no stripping). 1 coat on new wood with good absorption, 2 coats on weathered wood for color build. Most forgiving application — penetrating stain hides minor application inconsistencies. No primer required.

material_systems.notes: Standard residential recommendation. Best balance of protection, aesthetics, and maintainability. Coverage is porosity-dependent: new smooth wood achieves higher end of range, weathered/porous wood at lower end. Back-brushing mandatory when spray-applied to force stain into wood grain.

material_systems.name: Semi-Solid Stain

stain.notes: Enhanced UV protection with heavier pigment load. Thin film allows some vapor transmission — better moisture management than solid stain. Partially masks wood grain (texture visible, grain pattern obscured). 3-4 year maintenance cycle. Good for hiding wood imperfections, color inconsistencies, or previous stain color underneath. Two coats standard. No primer required — thin-film penetrating chemistry.

material_systems.notes: Middle ground between semi-transparent and solid. Higher coverage rate than semi-transparent due to film-forming component reducing absorption into wood. Useful for color change over previous stain or covering cosmetic wood defects.

material_systems.name: Solid Color Deck Stain

stain.type: Film-forming solid body stain — opaque color, complete grain masking
products: Cabot Solid Color Acrylic Deck Stain
stain.notes: Maximum UV protection — film-forming coating essentially behaves like paint. Opaque color completely masks wood grain. 5-7 year cycle on vertical surfaces. WARNING: HIGHEST DELAMINATION RISK on horizontal walking surfaces — moisture-driven peeling is the #1 failure mode for film-forming coatings on decks. Two coats mandatory with full dry between coats. May require tannin-blocking primer on cedar/redwood substrates.

material_systems.notes: Not recommended as first choice for horizontal deck surfaces due to delamination risk. Best suited for vertical railing components where moisture entrapment is less severe. Closest to traditional paint behavior — requires more prep for maintenance recoat (sand, possibly strip). Tannin-blocking primer may be required on cedar/redwood. Coverage is higher than penetrating stains because film sits on surface rather than absorbing.

material_systems.name: Deck Cleaner / Stripper (Alkaline)

prep_chemical.type: Alkaline wood cleaner/stripper — sodium hydroxide or sodium percarbonate based, pH 12-14
products: Sherwin-Williams SuperDeck Revive Deck & Dock Cleaner
prep_chemical.notes: First step in chemical restoration protocol for weathered or previously coated wood. Removes failed coating residue, mildew, dirt, UV-degraded fiber, and opens wood pores. Apply with pump sprayer or brush, allow to dwell 10-15 minutes, scrub with stiff bristle brush, rinse with garden hose or low-pressure washer. MUST be neutralized with acid brightener (SYS_EXT_DECK_BRIGHTENER) before staining — alkaline residue prevents proper stain adhesion and penetration.

material_systems.notes: Not used on new bare wood (SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD) — new wood prep is mill glaze removal, not chemical stripping. Coverage varies by contamination level: heavily soiled/failed coatings consume more product.

material_systems.name: Wood Brightener (Oxalic / Citric Acid)

prep_chemical.type: Oxalic acid or citric acid wood brightener, pH 1.5-2.5
prep_chemical.notes: Second step in chemical restoration protocol. Neutralizes alkaline stripper residue, restores natural wood color by dissolving surface tannin deposits, and lowers wood surface pH to 3.5-4.5 (optimal for stain adhesion). Oxalic acid formula preferred for cedar/redwood tannin management. Citric acid as milder alternative. MANDATORY after alkaline stripping — never stain over alkaline residue. Also used standalone on cedar/redwood substrates (even new wood) to manage tannin bleed before staining. Apply with pump sprayer or brush, allow 10-15 minutes, rinse thoroughly. Allow 24-48 hours drying before staining.

material_systems.notes: On cedar/redwood, brightener is used even on new bare wood (SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD) for tannin management — this is the substrate_type_override scenario. On PT pine, brightener is only used after alkaline stripping (weathered/previously_coated conditions).

new_smooth.notes: New smooth wood (mill-prepped, glaze removed). Lower absorption — sealer sits closer to surface. Best coverage scenario.

new_rough_sawn.notes: New rough-sawn wood. Open fiber structure absorbs more product. Common on cedar and redwood.

weathered_restored.notes: Weathered wood after chemical restoration. Open pores from UV damage absorb more product despite restoration.

end_grain_modifier.notes: End-grain absorbs 2-3x more product than face grain. Apply factor to end-grain area estimates (stairs, board ends, railing post tops). Factor 0.40 means 40% of normal coverage = 2.5x material consumption.

assumptions: Coverage per single coat application with brush or pad applicator.
Spray_backbrush adds ~15% material for overspray and surface deposit before brushing in.
End-grain areas (stair treads, board ends, post tops) consume 2-3x normal — captured in end_grain_modifier.

new_smooth.notes: New smooth wood. Moderate absorption. Single coat typically sufficient on new wood with good mill glaze removal.

new_rough_sawn.notes: New rough-sawn wood. Higher absorption into open fiber structure.

weathered_restored.notes: Weathered wood after chemical restoration. Most porous condition — highest material consumption. Two coats typical for color build on weathered substrate.

end_grain_modifier.notes: End-grain absorbs 2-3x more stain. Factor 0.40 = ~2.5x material consumption on end-grain areas.

assumptions: Coverage per coat. New wood typically 1 coat, weathered wood typically 2 coats.
Oil-based semi-transparent stains and water-based stains have comparable coverage rates — open time differs but absorption is similar.

new_smooth.notes: New smooth wood. Film-forming component reduces absorption — higher coverage than semi-transparent.

new_rough_sawn.notes: Rough-sawn absorbs more product despite film-forming component.

weathered_restored.notes: Weathered restored wood. Porous substrate but thin-film builds up better than pure penetrating stain.

end_grain_modifier.notes: End-grain absorption is less severe with semi-solid (film-forming component) than pure penetrating stains. Factor 0.50 = ~2x material consumption on end-grain.

assumptions: Coverage per coat. Two coats standard for all wood conditions.
Higher coverage than semi-transparent due to film-forming component reducing wood absorption.

new_smooth.notes: New smooth wood. Film-forming product builds on surface — minimal absorption. Highest coverage of all deck coating types.

new_rough_sawn.notes: Rough-sawn texture increases surface area and absorbs some product before film forms.

weathered_restored.notes: Weathered restored wood. Porous substrate absorbs first coat more heavily. Second coat achieves better coverage.

end_grain_modifier.notes: End-grain absorption is least severe with solid stain (full film-forming). Factor 0.60 = ~1.7x material consumption on end-grain.

assumptions: Coverage per coat. Two coats mandatory with full dry between coats.
Spray_backbrush adds ~20% material for overspray (film-forming generates more mist than penetrating).
Solid stain coverage is comparable to exterior paint — film sits on surface rather than absorbing.

standard.notes: Coverage varies by contamination level. Heavily soiled or multi-layer failed coatings may require double application at lower end of range.

assumptions: Single application. May require second application on heavily contaminated surfaces.
Apply with pump sprayer or brush. Pump sprayer is more efficient for large areas.
Dwell time 10-15 minutes before scrubbing and rinsing.

standard.notes: Consistent coverage regardless of wood condition — acid brightener is applied evenly. Cedar/redwood may require slightly more product for tannin dissolution.

assumptions: Single application. Cedar/redwood tannin management may require extended dwell time but not necessarily more product.
Apply with pump sprayer or brush. Allow 10-15 minutes, rinse thoroughly.
24-48 hours drying after brightener application before staining.

consumables.name: Stain applicator pad (lamb's wool or synthetic)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 300-500 SF of floor field staining
consumables.notes: Primary applicator for deck floor staining with penetrating stains. Lamb's wool pads provide smooth, even application. Synthetic pads are more durable. Attaches to pad applicator handle (pole-length for standing application). Replace when pad becomes saturated/matted and no longer releases stain evenly.

consumables.name: Stiff synthetic bristle brush 4-6 inch (back-brush / stain application)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 500 SF of floor back-brushing or 100 LF of railing brushwork
consumables.notes: MANDATORY for spray_backbrush application — forces penetrating stain into wood grain pores. Also used as primary brush for railing and detail work. Stiff synthetic bristle (not soft-tip) for maximum stain working into grain. 4-6 inch width for floor field, 2-3 inch for railings and detail. Stain degrades bristles faster than paint — replace more frequently than paint brushes.

consumables.name: Detail brush 2-3 inch (railings, spindles, stairs)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per 50 LF of railing or 60 EA spindles
consumables.notes: Smaller brush for detail staining: railings, spindles, stair treads/risers, post tops. Stiff synthetic bristle. Replace when bristles soften or fray. High-detail work on spindles wears brushes faster.

consumables.name: Pump sprayer (2-gallon, for stain and prep chemical application)
consumables.notes: Hand-pump sprayer for applying penetrating stains (small-medium decks), chemical stripper, and acid brightener. NOT an airless sprayer — penetrating stains use pump sprayer or HVLP, not high-pressure airless (which atomizes too finely for penetrating products). Also used for applying chemical prep products. Clean between products — do NOT cross-contaminate alkaline stripper and acid brightener.

consumables.name: Sanding disc 60 grit (mill glaze removal)
consumables.notes: For mill glaze removal on new wood. Random orbital sander or palm sander. 60 grit opens sealed mill-glazed surface for stain penetration. Aggressive cut — used only for initial mill glaze breakthrough. Switch to 80 grit for smoothing after glaze is broken.

consumables.name: Sanding disc 80-100 grit (refinishing / fiber removal)
consumables.notes: For smoothing after mill glaze removal (80 grit) and removing loose fibers on weathered wood (100 grit). Random orbital sander. Also used for scuff-sanding between coats of solid stain if needed.

consumables.name: Random orbital sander rental (floor sanding)
consumables.notes: For deck floor sanding: mill glaze removal, weathered fiber removal, or solid stain prep. Random orbital (NOT belt sander — belt sander creates gouges on deck boards). 5-6 inch pad. Rental per day for floor sanding tasks. Not needed if chemical mill glaze removal is used instead of mechanical.

consumables.name: Pressure washer (1,500-2,000 PSI for deck cleaning)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 EA per project (daily rental or owned)
consumables.notes: For deck cleaning and rinsing chemical products. Fan tip (25-40 degree) at 1,500-2,000 PSI maximum for decks. WARNING: higher pressure (3,000+ PSI) damages wood fibers, creates fuzzy surface, and opens grain excessively. Keep nozzle 8-12 inches from surface. Sweep with the grain, never across or against. Used for cleaning existing decks and rinsing chemical restoration products.

consumables.name: Stiff bristle scrub brush (chemical prep)
consumables.notes: Heavy-duty stiff bristle push broom or deck scrub brush for working chemical stripper and brightener into wood surface. Poly or tampico bristle. Not wire (wire can embed in wood and rust-stain). Used during chemical restoration protocol dwell time to agitate product and lift contaminants.

consumables.name: Painter's tape (exterior grade, UV-resistant)
consumables.usage_rate: 1 ROLL (60 yd) per 30 LF of trim/siding masking lines
consumables.notes: UV-resistant exterior masking tape for protecting house trim at deck-to-house junction, siding at ledger board, and any smooth-surface fixtures. 14-day removal rating minimum. Standard blue painter's tape — stucco tape NOT needed (deck surfaces are smooth wood, not rough masonry). Reused consumable ID.

consumables.name: Plastic sheeting (4 mil, UV-resistant)
consumables.notes: For siding protection during spray operations (tape at ledger board, drape plastic down siding face 4-6 ft). Below-deck vegetation protection on elevated decks. Furniture covering when relocation is not possible. 4 mil minimum for durability. UV-resistant for multi-day projects.

consumables.name: Canvas drop cloths
consumables.notes: For protecting adjacent hardscape (walkways, patios, concrete pads) from stain drip and overspray. Non-slip surface for crew traffic. Also used below elevated deck perimeter when plastic alone is insufficient. Reused consumable ID.

consumables.name: Stir sticks and mixing containers
consumables.usage_rate: 2 EA stir sticks per gallon + 1 mixing bucket per 5 gallons
consumables.notes: Penetrating stains require thorough stirring before and during application — pigments settle faster than in latex paint. Box multiple gallons in a 5-gallon bucket for color consistency across the deck. Stir sticks per gallon opened. Mixing bucket for boxing.

consumables.name: Pin-type electronic moisture meter (verification tool)
consumables.notes: MANDATORY verification tool. Electronic pin-type moisture meter for wood MC reading. MC must be < 15% before any stain application (HARD STOP if above). Take readings at 6-8 locations across deck surface (center, edges, shaded areas, areas near ground). Water bead test is supplemental field check only — moisture meter is authoritative.

ext_siding_adjacent.description: House siding at deck-to-house junction (ledger board area)
ext_siding_adjacent.notes: Brush application: tape at ledger board junction. Spray_backbrush: plastic sheeting on siding face from deck level up 4-6 ft, taped at top edge. Protection level escalates with application method (light_mask → full_cover for spray).

ext_landscape_below_deck.description: Vegetation and landscaping below elevated deck perimeter
ext_landscape_below_deck.notes: Drop cloth/tarp below elevated deck perimeter to catch drips and overspray falling through board gaps. Ground-level decks have minimal below-deck concern. LF along deck perimeter.

ext_hardscape_adjacent.description: Adjacent walkways, patios, concrete pads at ground level
ext_hardscape_adjacent.notes: Canvas drop cloths for non-slip crew traffic areas. Plastic sheeting for overspray protection on areas without foot traffic. Stain drip from deck edge onto hardscape is difficult to remove.

ext_deck_furniture.description: On-deck furniture, planters, grills requiring relocation or covering
ext_deck_furniture.notes: Move furniture off deck entirely (preferred) or consolidate and cover with plastic. Not a masking task — relocation/staging. Per furniture group or section. Unique to deck scope — items ON the surface being stained.

ext_light_fixture.notes: Bag or tape over fixture with plastic during staining. Remove fixture cover plate if accessible. Use blue tape on fixture surfaces (smooth).

compatibility_rules.description: Moisture content must be below 15% before any coating application
compatibility_rules.required_action: Moisture test with pin-type electronic moisture meter. MC > 15% = HARD STOP — do not stain. Reschedule.
compatibility_rules.notes: MC above 15% prevents stain penetration into wood fibers (penetrating stains) and causes adhesion failure (solid stain). Electronic pin-type moisture meter is the authoritative measurement. Water bead test is supplemental field check only.

compatibility_rules.description: New pressure-treated pine requires 3-6 month seasoning before staining
compatibility_rules.required_action: HARD STOP if wood age < 3 months. Verify seasoning with builder/GC. 6 months preferred.
compatibility_rules.notes: New PT lumber contains waterborne preservatives (ACQ, CA-B, MCA) that leave wood saturated with copper compounds and moisture. Staining green PT wood results in poor penetration, blotchy appearance, and premature coating failure. This is a project-level gate — verify BEFORE scheduling.

compatibility_rules.description: Solid stain on horizontal deck surfaces = delamination risk WARNING
compatibility_rules.required_action: Document delamination risk in project record. Recommend semi-transparent or semi-solid as alternative. Proceed only with customer acknowledgment.
compatibility_rules.notes: Film-forming solid stain on horizontal walking surfaces is the #1 failure mode for deck coatings. Moisture enters through cracks, end-grain, and fastener holes, becomes trapped under film, and causes blistering and sheet delamination. Foot traffic accelerates failure. Not a hard stop, but must be documented. Solid stain is safer on vertical railing components.

compatibility_rules.description: Cedar/redwood requires oxalic acid brightener for tannin management
compatibility_rules.notes: Cedar and redwood contain water-soluble extractive tannins that bleed through coatings causing dark brown/red discoloration. Oxalic acid brightener dissolves surface tannins before staining. MANDATORY on cedar/redwood regardless of wood condition. Oil-based stains resist tannin bleed better than water-based on these substrates.

compatibility_rules.description: Never apply stain over degraded gray wood without restoration
compatibility_rules.required_action: Chemical restoration (SYS_EXT_DECK_CHEMICAL_STRIPPER + SYS_EXT_DECK_BRIGHTENER) OR mechanical sanding required before staining.
compatibility_rules.notes: UV-degraded gray wood has loose cellulose fibers and degraded lignin on the surface. Stain applied over gray wood bonds to loose fibers, not sound wood — coating fails prematurely as loose fibers detach. Chemical restoration or sanding removes degraded surface layer to expose sound wood for stain penetration.

compatibility_rules.description: Alkaline stripper must be neutralized with acid brightener before staining
compatibility_rules.notes: Alkaline wood cleaner/stripper (pH 12-14) leaves alkaline residue on wood surface. Alkaline residue prevents proper stain adhesion and penetration. Acid brightener (pH 1.5-2.5) neutralizes alkaline residue and restores wood surface pH to 3.5-4.5 (optimal for stain adhesion). NEVER skip brightener step after alkaline stripping.

compatibility_rules.description: Mill glaze removal mandatory on all new wood before staining
compatibility_rules.required_action: Chemical mill glaze remover (preferred) or mechanical sanding (60-80 grit). Verify with water absorption test — water should absorb within 30 seconds.
compatibility_rules.notes: Mill glaze is a burnished, shiny surface created by sawmill planing. Seals wood surface and prevents stain penetration. All new wood substrates (PT pine, cedar, redwood) have mill glaze to some degree. Chemical remover is preferred (less aggressive, does not alter wood profile). Mechanical sanding (60-80 grit) as alternative.

compatibility_rules.description: Penetrating stains do NOT use primer
compatibility_rules.notes: Primer seals the wood surface and PREVENTS stain penetration — the opposite of the desired effect. Penetrating stains (clear, semi-transparent, semi-solid) must be applied directly to bare or prepared wood. The traditional prime-then-paint pipeline does not apply to penetrating deck stains.

risk_notes.topic: Solid stain delamination on horizontal walking surfaces
risk_notes.risk: Solid stain (film-forming) on horizontal deck surfaces traps moisture from rain, snow, and irrigation entering through cracks, end-grain, and fastener holes. Water becomes trapped between wood and film, causing blistering and sheet delamination. Foot traffic abrades the weakened film. This is the most common and most severe deck coating failure mode. Horizontal surfaces collect 10-100x more water than vertical surfaces.
risk_notes.mitigation: Recommend penetrating stains (semi-transparent or semi-solid) for horizontal deck surfaces. If solid stain is specified, document delamination risk in project record with customer acknowledgment. Ensure all fastener holes and end-grain are sealed. Verify MC < 15% before application.

risk_notes.topic: Premature erosion from insufficient stain penetration
risk_notes.risk: Penetrating stain applied to wood with mill glaze, excess moisture (MC > 15%), or insufficient surface preparation sits on the surface rather than penetrating into wood fibers. Surface-sitting stain erodes within weeks to months instead of the expected 2-3 year cycle. Most common on new PT pine that has not been properly seasoned or prepped.
risk_notes.mitigation: Remove mill glaze on all new wood (chemical or 60-80 grit sanding). Verify MC < 15% with electronic moisture meter. Verify PT pine has seasoned 3-6 months. Perform water absorption test. Back-brush when spray-applying to force stain into grain.

risk_notes.risk: Water-soluble extractive tannins in cedar and redwood bleed through coatings, causing dark brown/red discoloration. Most severe with water-based coatings and at end-grain locations. Tannin stains surrounding surfaces (concrete walkways, house siding below deck) and discolors the coating itself.
risk_notes.mitigation: Treat cedar/redwood with oxalic acid brightener before staining to dissolve surface tannins. Consider oil-based stain for better tannin resistance. For solid stain, use tannin-blocking primer. For clear/semi-transparent coatings, accept some tannin bleed as normal aesthetic with natural wood look.

risk_notes.topic: Alligatoring from over-application of penetrating stain
risk_notes.risk: Excessive stain application (too much product, insufficient back-brushing, pooling in low spots) creates a thick surface film on what should be a penetrating coating. The thick film cracks in an alligator-skin pattern as wood expands and contracts seasonally. Common on end-grain areas that absorb unevenly, board joints, and low spots where product pools.
risk_notes.mitigation: Apply thin coats. Maintain wet edge. Back-brush thoroughly to work stain into wood and remove excess. Do not allow puddles or pooling. Apply second coat only after first has absorbed (30-60 minutes for penetrating stains). Monitor end-grain and joint areas for excess buildup.

risk_notes.risk: Pressure washing at too high PSI (>2,000 for softwood decks) or too close distance damages wood fibers, creates fuzzy raised grain, gouges surface, and opens grain excessively. Damaged wood absorbs stain unevenly, creating blotchy appearance. Pressure washer damage is common on PT pine (soft wood).
risk_notes.mitigation: Maximum 1,500-2,000 PSI with fan tip (25-40 degree) for deck cleaning. Keep nozzle 8-12 inches from surface. Sweep WITH the grain, never across or against. Never use zero-degree (turbo) nozzle on wood. If wood fibers are raised by pressure washing, light sanding (80-100 grit) required before staining.

risk_notes.risk: Alkaline stripper (pH 12-14) and acid brightener (pH 1.5-2.5) are chemically incompatible. Cross-contamination in pump sprayers, brushes, or mixing containers causes neutralization reaction that renders both products ineffective. Using acid brightener residue-contaminated sprayer for alkaline stripper (or vice versa) wastes product and fails to achieve desired chemical action.
risk_notes.mitigation: Use dedicated pump sprayers for alkaline and acid products — label clearly. Rinse all application tools thoroughly between products. Allow alkaline stripper to be fully rinsed from surface before applying acid brightener.

risk_notes.topic: Below-deck stain drip on elevated decks
risk_notes.risk: Stain applied to deck floor drips through gaps between deck boards onto landscaping, vehicles, patio furniture, and other surfaces below. Penetrating stain on vegetation or hardscape is extremely difficult to remove. Elevated decks (4+ ft above grade) have greater drift distance for dripping stain.
risk_notes.mitigation: Full below-deck protection (plastic sheeting, drop cloths) on elevated decks. Notify homeowner to move vehicles from below-deck areas. Check below deck after staining for drip penetration through protection.

material_quantity_notes.spray_transfer_efficiency: Pump sprayer for penetrating stains: ~80-85% transfer efficiency (low-pressure, minimal overspray). Airless sprayer for solid stain: ~65-75% transfer efficiency. Back-brushing redistributes overspray — actual material waste is lower than wall spraying because excess is worked into wood.
material_quantity_notes.wood_porosity_factor: New smooth wood: 1.00x. New rough-sawn: 1.25-1.50x. Weathered/restored: 1.30-1.50x. Applied on top of base coverage rate. Porosity modifier affects stain coats primarily — prep chemicals have flatter coverage profiles.
material_quantity_notes.end_grain_factor: End-grain (stair treads, board ends, post tops, railing joints) absorbs 2-3x more product than face grain. Budget additional material for decks with many stairs or exposed end-grain. Critical for accurate material ordering.
material_quantity_notes.coat_count_by_system: Clear sealer: 1 coat. Semi-transparent: 1 coat (new wood), 2 coats (weathered). Semi-solid: 2 coats (all conditions). Solid stain: 2 coats mandatory with full dry between. Chemical stripper: 1 application. Brightener: 1 application.
material_quantity_notes.component_material_distribution: Typical 400 SF deck with 60 LF railing, 30 spindles, 6 stairs: ~80% of stain material goes to floor field, ~12% to railings, ~5% to spindles (small area per unit), ~3% to stairs. Material ordering should be based on floor field SF plus component supplements.
material_quantity_notes.boxing_requirement: CRITICAL: Box (mix) all gallons of stain into a single container before application to ensure color consistency. Penetrating stain color varies slightly between cans. Boxing eliminates lot-to-lot variation across the deck surface.

assumptions.value: 150-300 SF/gal for penetrating stains, varying by coating type, wood condition, and wood species
assumptions.note: Doctrine provides general ranges. Coverage profiles refined by wood condition (new smooth vs rough-sawn vs weathered) based on wood porosity and absorption characteristics. Conservative midpoints used for estimation.

assumptions.value: 200-400 SF/gal — higher than penetrating stains due to film-forming (surface-sitting) chemistry
assumptions.note: Solid stain behaves like paint — builds film on surface rather than absorbing. Coverage is comparable to exterior paint on smooth surfaces.

assumptions.value: 150-250 SF/gal for alkaline stripper and acid brightener
assumptions.note: Doctrine does not specify exact coverage rates for deck chemical prep products. Derived from manufacturer product data sheets and field experience. Flag for field calibration.

assumptions.value: End-grain absorbs 2-3x more product than face grain
assumptions.note: Doctrine mentions end-grain absorption risk but does not quantify the multiplier. 2-3x is wood science standard for softwood end-grain vs face-grain absorption. Flag for field calibration on stair-heavy decks.

assumptions.value: Standard blue painter's tape is adequate for deck masking — red stucco poly tape NOT required
assumptions.note: Deck surfaces are smooth wood, not rough masonry. Standard blue tape adheres properly to smooth wood, house trim, and siding. Stucco tape is a masonry-specific consumable.

assumptions.value: Pump sprayer (or HVLP) for penetrating stain application — NOT airless sprayer
assumptions.note: Penetrating stains are best applied with low-pressure methods (pump sprayer, HVLP) that deposit product without excessive atomization. Airless sprayers over-atomize penetrating products. Solid stain CAN use airless (film-forming product). Flag for explicit doctrine guidance.

uncertainty_flags.description: End-grain absorbs 2-3x more stain than face grain — this is well-established wood science. However, the exact multiplier varies by wood species, moisture content, and stain chemistry. On stair-heavy decks (10+ steps), end-grain material consumption significantly impacts total material order.
uncertainty_flags.impact: Material ordering may be short by 15-25% on stair-heavy decks if end-grain consumption is underestimated.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: Field measurement data from 3-5 deck projects comparing actual stain consumption vs theoretical coverage on decks with varying stair counts.

uncertainty_flags.topic: Oil-based vs water-based stain coverage difference
uncertainty_flags.description: Coverage profiles do not differentiate between oil-based and water-based stains. Oil-based stains may have slightly different absorption profiles (deeper penetration, different solids content). Most professional products have converged on similar coverage rates, but field variation exists.
uncertainty_flags.impact: Low — coverage ranges are wide enough to accommodate both chemistries. Boxing requirement and field ordering should adjust.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: If doctrine establishes oil-based vs water-based stain distinction, split coverage profiles accordingly.

uncertainty_flags.description: Alkaline stripper and acid brightener coverage rates (150-250 SF/gal) are derived from manufacturer PDS data. Actual field coverage varies significantly by contamination level, number of failed coating layers, and dwell time. Heavily contaminated surfaces may require double application.
uncertainty_flags.impact: Chemical prep material ordering may be off by 25-50% on heavily contaminated decks.
uncertainty_flags.resolution_needed: Field calibration data from weathered deck restoration projects. Consider adding contamination_level modifier to coverage profile.
